newsitem.title: CHINA: HK head Tung visits Beijing as political woes grow.
newsitem.headline: HK head Tung visits Beijing as political woes grow.

text.p: Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa departed for Beijing on Friday amid bitter disputes over his handling of the media, a crackdown on young Chinese migrants, and legal challenges to his administration.
Less than two weeks after its return to Chinese rule, Hong Kong is embroiled in a nasty quarrel, with local media accusing Tung of giving preferred treatment to mainland Chinese media.

The Hong Kong Journalists Association wrote to Tung's office on Thursday complaining that local media were excluded from covering Tung's first meeting with China's garrison commander last week, while mainland TV crews had complete access.
Tung's office denied the accusations. "We are not giving preferential treatment to anybody. We did not deliberately exclude anyone," a Tung spokesman told Reuters on Friday.
He said Tung's officials were themselves taken aback when they saw the Chinese had arranged media coverage on their end.
The spokesman also said Tung had now sought to improve communications with the Chinese and had urged senior Chinese officials to be more aware of local media sensitivities.
"He has talked to them about improving the arrangements for media and of paying attention to the media perception.
"They agreed. In most cases, this just hasn't occurred to people (the Chinese)," the spokesman said.
Tung flew off to Beijing to attend a key meeting to wind up the Preparatory Committee, the body that steered the return of this ex-British colony to China on July 1.
His first week or so in office has been a rough ride.

An illegal influx of mainland Chinese children trying to join parents already here has prompted Tung to ram through a law allowing the deportation of thousands of young migrants who sneaked into the territory in recent years.
But the new law, enacted on Wednesday by the China-appointed Provisional Legislature, has been harshly criticised by lawyers, welfare pressure groups and human rights monitors.
They say it contravenes Hong Kong's constitution which provides that children born out of the territory have residency right so long as one or both parents are permanent residents.
Parents of dozens of these children facing deportation have already applied for legal aid to fight the new law and at least 10 lawyers have indicated they will offer their services free.
The Provisional Legislature itself is also under attack as it faces a court hearing later this month challenging its legitimacy.
The 60-member body, made up of pro-China, business figures and which has no representation from the popular Democratic Party, replaced an elected legislature on July 1.
It has passed laws rolling back civil liberties for this territory of 6.4 million and has now been asked by the government to suspend a clutch of laws protecting labour rights.
To make things worse, the United States said on Thursday it would not recognise laws passed by the body.
Meanwhile, China's top official on Hong Kong affairs, Lu Ping, whose hallmark the new Hong Kong government carries, has said in Beijing he is retiring, Hong Kong radio reported.
Lu will be replaced next week by Liao Hui, head of the Overseas Chinese Affairs Office under China's State Council, Chinese sources said.
